extracted.intended_audience: students and readers interested in the history of advertising; historians of print culture
extracted.subtask_description: A book-chapter style historical account describing the development and variety of seventeenth-century advertisements in British newspapers and periodicals, with many excerpted examples and commentary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advertisements as multifunctional public notices
rubrics_metrics.description: Advertisements serve many public functions — lost-and-found notices, rewards for discovery, announcements of assaults and calls for discovery of offenders, sales and lettings of property, insurance society notices, employment/servant advertisements, sales of books and sermons, and commercial offers (quack medicines, goods).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The chapter repeatedly illustrates how advertisements functioned as the public medium for practical notices (e.g., lost diamond, lost goose and gander), legal/criminal appeals (offers of reward and pardon for discovery of Dryden's assailants), commercial offers (Daffy's Elixir), property and letting notices (Earl of Berkeley's house), insurance calls for contributions, and employment wants. Example extracts from the London Gazette, Domestick Intelligence, Flying Post, and others are used to demonstrate the range.

rubrics_metrics.name: Detailed physical description as an ad device
rubrics_metrics.description: Lost-persons, runaway servants, animals, and thieves are described with precise physical detail (colouring, marks, clothing, rings, periwig, spurs, etc.) to aid identification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: the 'Goose and Gander' described by head, back, wings, spurs, beaks and legs; 'Thomas Gooseberry, a blackamoor ... wears a periwig'; runaway 'Obdelah Elias Abraham' with 'gold ring in his ear' and clothing listed. The text shows advertisers relied on specific physical markers to make notices useful and credible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monetary rewards and deposited funds as credibility/encouragement
rubrics_metrics.description: Offers of monetary reward — sometimes with money deposited in known hands — are used to incentivize informants and signal seriousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: ten pounds for lost diamond; fifty pounds deposited with a goldsmith for discovery of Dryden's attackers; guinea rewards for apprehending runaways or thieves. The deposit-with-goldsmith detail (Blanchard, Goldsmith) functions as a trust signal and proof the reward exists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal/political incentives and promises (pardons, royal commands)
rubrics_metrics.description: Advertisements can include legal or political inducements such as royal promises of pardon or statements that publication is 'by His Majesty's Command.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrations: 'his Majesty is graciously pleased to promise him his pardon' for discoverers; publication of sermons 'Published by His Majesty's Command.' Such provisions show advertisers used official/legal levers to reinforce the ad's authority or attract compliance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Format and distribution channels of advertisements
rubrics_metrics.description: Ads appear in a variety of printed formats and outlets: government Gazettes, small newspapers (Domestick Intelligence, Flying Post), single leaves printed back and front, and hybrid printed-manuscript sheets sold for private correspondence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The chapter notes a single leaf printed back and front (a complete newspaper leaf), newspapers printed with double dates, and the 'sheet of fine paper' sold by J. Salusbury that combined public news and space for private writing. It stresses the practical and commercial roles of these formats in reaching readers (city and country audiences).

rubrics_metrics.name: Blending of newspaper and private letter (news-sheet hybrids)
rubrics_metrics.description: Publishers sold printed sheets with half blank so readers could add private business — a hybrid between newspaper and letter to serve country correspondents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Flying Post (1694) offered an account of public affairs for two-pence on a sheet 'half of which being blank, he may thereon write his own private business.' The chapter explains this combined the newspaper and private letter and suited country readers craving metropolitan gossip.

rubrics_metrics.name: Branding and authenticity signals (seals, sole-preparation claims)
rubrics_metrics.description: Sellers claim exclusive right/validity and use physical seals or statements of sole preparation to assert authenticity (e.g., 'the true Elixir Salutis ... sealed with his seal').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Daffy's Elixir advertises that the 'true' cordial is 'to be sold' only at specified places and that printed sheets are 'sealed with his seal.' The narrative highlights such signals as a method to counter counterfeiters and to confer trust.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of sensational and emotive language to attract attention
rubrics_metrics.description: Advertisements and notices employ vivid, sensational language (barbarously assaulted, murther, whipping, hanging of Protestants) to engage readers and emphasize urgency or outrage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The chapter quotes contemporary reports and 'Orange Cards' that enumerate dramatic events and uses the Domestick Intelligence's language recounting the assault on Dryden to show how emotive phrasing served to capture public interest and shape perception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clear calls-to-action and contact points
rubrics_metrics.description: Notices conclude with explicit instructions on how to respond (bring to X, enquire of Y, give notice to Mr Z) and named contact persons/locations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'is required to bring it to William Chiffinch, Esq., Keeper of his Majesty's Closet'; 'Whoever brings him to Mr Lozel's house ... shall have one guinea.' The presence of named individuals and locations functioned as the ad's actionable endpoint.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of authority/office/titles as credibility cues
rubrics_metrics.description: Ads rely on the social standing or official position of named persons (keepers, esquires, knights, publishers) to lend weight and credibility to notices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notices reference titles: 'Keeper of his Majesty's Closet', 'Sir Thomas Fowles, goldsmith', 'Mr John Martin at Guildhall Coffeehouse', publishers like 'Donnan Newman' and editors like Bishop Burnet — the text emphasizes how social rank and named officials reinforced trustworthiness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advertisements as instruments of political/religious propaganda and celebration
rubrics_metrics.description: Printed items sold via the press (cards, prints, sermons) are used to celebrate political events, denounce opponents, and propagate partisan narratives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'ORANGE CARDS' listing anti-Jacobite scenes and 'efigies of our Gracious K. William & Q. Mary' sold by the New Observator's publisher. The chapter explains such items were popular ways to commemorate and promote political triumphs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Administrative notices with deadlines and contribution rates
rubrics_metrics.description: Groups use advertisements to call members to make payments, stating specific rates and deadlines (e.g., insurance society asking members to pay proportions by a date).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustration: Friendly society fire losses notice specifying 'five shillings and one penny for every hundred pounds insured, before the 12th of August next.' The text shows ads were a vehicle for operational, civic management communications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Employment ads specifying qualifications, security and conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: Job/service advertisements list desired skills, personal history (e.g., had small-pox), language ability, required character references or security (bonds), and salary expectations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Houghton's notices ask for an Englishman who can 'tolerably well speak French (if Dutch too so much the better)', or a servant 'has had the small-pox, and can give some small security for his honesty.' Another applicant offers to give security 'as far as ten thousand pounds' for a salary — demonstrating detailed employment ad requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advertising supply and topical composition in papers
rubrics_metrics.description: Newspaper ad pages are not crowded with commercial notices in this period; columns are often dominated by booksellers and quack notices, with only a few other adverts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The chapter notes 'rarely more than two or three at most beyond the booksellers' and quack notices,' highlighting the limited commercial advertising market and the thematic skew of columns in late seventeenth-century papers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of printed images and engravings to enhance appeal
rubrics_metrics.description: Publishers use engraved figures and lively illustrations (cards, prints) to depict events and augment the sales appeal of political and commemorative items.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Orange Cards are described as 'curiously illustrated and engraven in lively figures' — the chapter uses this example to show the early use of imagery in promotional items to attract purchasers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advertisements reflecting and reinforcing social prejudices or hierarchies
rubrics_metrics.description: Notices often encode and perpetuate contemporary social attitudes (hatred of Popery, treatment of 'blackamoor' servants as property, collars with owners' names), thus serving social as well as commercial functions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The commentary points to burial notices near executed Jesuits, runaway 'black' children with collars reading 'The Lady Bromfield's black', and discussion of popular hatred of Roman Catholicism — showing how ads could express or enforce prevailing social norms and prejudices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pricing and monetization practices for news and printed sheets
rubrics_metrics.description: Publishers experimented with pricing models (two-pence a sheet, annual subscriptions of three or four pounds for written news) to monetize news and newsletters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Salusbury's two-pence sheet in Cornhill; editors reminding readers that 'three or four pounds a year' must be paid for written news. The chapter uses these data points to illustrate emerging business practices around printed news.
